newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia's pro-euthanasia leaders vow to fight on.
newsitem.headline: Australia's pro-euthanasia leaders vow to fight on.

text.p: Pro-euthanasia leaders on Tuesday condemned Australian politicians, including Prime Minister John Howard, for voting to smother the world's first mercy killing law, but vowed to continue the fight for its survival.

"I am disgusted that these people who have been elected to represent the electorate failed to represent the beliefs of the people," Linda Cracknell, president of the Voluntary Euthanasia Network, told Reuters.

Opinion polls show around 75 percent of Australians support voluntary euthanasia. But early on Tuesday the Australian parliament's lower house, the House of Representatives, voted 88 to 35 in favour of a bill aimed at overthrowing a voluntary euthanasia law in the outback Northern Territory.
"The people of Australia have clearly indicated in opinion polls and surveys that they support the Northern Territory law on voluntary euthanasia by about 75 percent," Cracknell said.
"When you have 75 percent of the parliament voting to overturn the voluntary euthanasia law it indicates that parliament is not representative of the people."
The anti-euthanasia bill will go before the upper house Senate next year for final approval.
Dr Philip Nitschke, dubbed "Doctor death" by anti-euthanasia groups for assisting the first voluntary death in September, said the vote created uncertainty for terminally-ill patients seeking death.
"It does not create an atmosphere for a stampede, but it creates uncertainty and that is not helpful for the terminally ill," Nitschke told Reuters.

Nitschke said he had spoken to 40 people seeking to use the law since September, but only five were currently seeking the medical signatures necessary to use the law. "Everyone is anxious, but aware we have not yet lost," he said.
Nitschke said pro-euthanasia groups would soon begin a public campaign, including advertising, to pressure senators to reject the anti-euthanasia bill.

"The battle was always going to be fought in the Senate and we are about to launch an ideas campaign to awaken public opinion," Nitschke said. "Seventy five percent of people want this legislation to remain."

The world's first voluntary euthanasia law came into effect in July in the Northern Territory. In September, Australian cancer patient Bob Dent, 66, became the first and only person to use the law through a computer-delivered lethal injection.
Euthanasia is illegal in the rest of Australia, although many doctors concede that it is carried out unofficially.

With both conservative prime minister Howard and Labor opposition leader Kim Beazley opposing euthanasia, the national parliament was given a conscience vote on a private member's bill aimed at overturning the law.
The national parliament can overturn laws in Australia's three territories, but not its six states.
The bill will go before the upper house Senate early next year, where it could face a tougher battle.
However, Right to Life Australia welcomed the vote as a "monumental historic and social significance for the whole of Australia".
Margaret Tighe, chairwoman of Right to Life Australia, said the vote sent a clear message to Australia's states and territories not to introduce voluntary euthanasia laws.

"If the bill had been rejected by the House of Representatives, it would have been a black day indeed for Australia and for those Australians whose lives would be most at risk if euthanasia were legalised," Tighe said.
